target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers for low-income workers by giving people the day off.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, and retail/service jobs held by many low-income workers would often still operate. So the holiday would not reliably remove scheduling barriers for those workers and could leave them still unable to vote without wage loss or job risk.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday is a broadly effective way to increase turnout.
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout reform compared with other voting-access changes, so the holiday is unlikely to be a strong standalone solution.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would disadvantage low-income workers because schools would no longer provide childcare/supervision for dependents.
objection: For low-income caregivers, school closure on Election Day can actually reduce childcare and supervision conflicts, making it easier to vote rather than harder.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would not help low-income workers because wage loss/job risk remains the key barrier.
objection: Many low-income workers face not just wage loss but also caregiving and scheduling constraints; predictable school/work closure or flexibility from a holiday reduces those conflicts and therefore improves their ability to vote.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday would not reliably remove scheduling barriers because private employers are not forced to close.
objection: Even without a mandate for every employer, a national holiday creates predictable staffing patterns and widespread schedule flexibility, which in practice makes voting easier than on an ordinary workday.

target: AG2's claim that wage loss/job risk is the central barrier for low-income workers and that holiday-linked arrangements don't help.
objection: The real barrier is that low-income workers may lose wages or face job consequences when taking time off; holiday status commonly brings holiday pay, premiums, or greater flexibility, which can reduce that cost relative to an ordinary workday.

target: AG1's claim that holiday-linked employer practices reduce the wage-loss/job-risk barrier.
objection: Holiday pay or premiums usually reward working on the holiday, not taking time off to vote, so if a worker still has to leave a scheduled shift they can still lose wages or face job consequences. Therefore the holiday does not reliably remove the barrier.

target: AG1's assumption that holiday premiums make the policy better for low-income workers.
objection: For low-income workers with little financial slack, premium pay can make the cost of missing work more deterrent, not less, because the wages they forgo on a holiday may be higher than on an ordinary day.

target: AG2's proposal to rely on state-level employer time-off rules instead of a national holiday.
objection: State rules vary widely and leave many workers unprotected, so patchwork state reforms cannot reliably eliminate scheduling conflicts nationwide the way a federal holiday can.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is not equitable in practice because some wage-loss/job-risk remains.
objection: Even if some employers still create costs, a national holiday reduces overall scheduling conflicts nationwide and thereby addresses the core barrier pathway for many low-income voters rather than disadvantaging them overall.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would not help because workplaces may still operate.
objection: If schools and many workplaces close or run on reduced schedules, many low-income workers no longer need to miss work to vote, so the holiday does reduce the wage-loss/job-risk component for many of them.

target: AG2's claim that holiday pay can make wage loss worse for low-income workers.
objection: If workers can vote while working part of a premium-paid holiday shift, the higher pay offsets some of the lost time and reduces the net deterrent cost of voting, rather than strengthening it.

target: AG1's claim that reducing day-of scheduling conflicts is enough to support a holiday even if other barriers remain.
objection: A holiday only changes Election Day conditions; it does not automatically fix pre-Election Day barriers like registration problems, so it misses important obstacles some voters face.

target: AG1's claim that automatic voter registration is not a substitute because the day-of barrier matters too.
objection: Automatic voter registration directly removes pre-Election Day registration barriers, which a one-day holiday leaves in place, so it is a more reliable turnout reform.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday helps because many people are already registered and just need time off.
objection: Even if some voters are already registered, that does not make a holiday a good general reform, because many others still face pre-Election Day administrative barriers and the holiday does not solve them.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday broadly reduces day-of scheduling conflicts for ready voters.
objection: A holiday does not require private employers to close or give paid time off, so for many low-wage workers the same day-of scheduling barriers remain and turnout gains would be uneven across income groups.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is not worth adopting because it does not solve every voting barrier.
objection: A policy can still be worthwhile if it meaningfully reduces one major barrier for many eligible voters; it does not need to eliminate every obstacle to be an improvement.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday reduces the practical polling-hours barrier by changing work/school schedules.
objection: A federal holiday only changes the calendar; it does not automatically change polling hours or other election-time windows, so many workers may still need protected availability that the holiday does not guarantee.

target: AG1's assumption that holiday status reliably increases real-world availability during polling hours.
objection: Because private employers are not required to provide paid time off or close, workers may still be scheduled during polling hours, especially low-income workers in holiday-operating jobs, so the holiday does not reliably make them available to vote.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday meaningfully reduces the time-window barrier for many workers.
objection: If a proposed reform does not reliably remove the main barrier for low-income voters, it is not a dependable or equity-enhancing turnout strategy by itself, and state employer time-off rules are a better direct fix.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday typically lets many workers be free during polling hours because schools and workplaces close or flex.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or to provide paid time off, so workplaces can remain open and workers can still be scheduled during polling hours, leaving the core availability problem in place.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday reliably reduces the time-window barrier for low-income workers.
objection: Because low-income workers are disproportionately in jobs that keep operating on holidays, the holiday's effect on availability is uneven and the key scheduling deterrent often remains intact for the people most affected.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday is the appropriate policy because it removes scheduling barriers.
objection: A better policy is one that directly targets time off when workers need it, such as state employer time-off requirements, rather than relying on a calendar-only holiday that may leave the main barrier untouched.
